label: A compromised host vs a host that only shows the effects

mentor.diagnosis: You selected hosts that appear in the incident rather than hosts with evidence of compromise. Scoping too widely is as wrong as scoping too narrowly, and it costs far more: every host you wrongly include gets rebuilt.
contrast: Malicious file written, new autostart service, or unknown persistence
Beaconing outbound from a process on that host
The host is executing attacker code
Security log gap during the incident window
Something on the host removed the evidence
High CPU, slow response, session exhaustion
It is being hammered by compromised hosts
Inbound connections from a compromised host
It is the destination, not the source
Large file read by a stolen account
The credential was compromised, not the server
Attack attempt that was blocked and never executed
Recorded the traffic as a proxy or a log server
mentor.rule: Ask what is resident ON the host. Artefacts, persistence, or outbound activity originating there means compromised. Load, inbound connections, or a record of someone else's activity means affected.
mentor.tell: 'Scan clean, no unexpected files, no new services' is the phrase the exam uses to tell you a host is a victim rather than a casualty. Believe it.
mentor.trap: Servers at the centre of the story feel compromised because they are named constantly and are visibly suffering. The file server whose data was stolen with a valid credential was never compromised at all.

label: Which log answers which question in an investigation

mentor.diagnosis: You picked the source that sounded most authoritative rather than the one that can actually hold the answer. Each log sees one layer, and a question about a layer it cannot see has no answer there however complete the log is.
contrast: Which flows were allowed or denied, between which addresses and ports
What was inside the traffic, or which user
Which traffic matched a signature or deviated from a baseline, and whether it was blocked
Anything it has no signature or baseline for
Who talked to whom, how much and for how long
Anything not captured at the time, and nothing useful if encrypted
Logons, privilege use, account and policy changes on that host
What a process did to files or the network
Process lineage, file writes, persistence, outbound connections per process
Activity on hosts without an agent
What the application itself did: transactions, errors, who requested what
Who, when, where and how large, without the content
mentor.rule: Ask which layer the question lives at. 'Was it allowed through' is the firewall, 'what ran' is the endpoint, 'who signed in' is the OS security log, 'what did the user do in the system' is the application log.
mentor.tell: An investigation question naming a specific thing to establish, with four plausible log sources offered.
mentor.trap: Packet capture feels like the complete answer and is usually wrong: it only exists if someone was capturing at that point beforehand, and most traffic is encrypted anyway.

label: Dashboards and automated reports vs the underlying log data

mentor.diagnosis: You treated a dashboard as a data source. A dashboard is a view over data someone already chose to collect, aggregate and keep, and all three of those decisions can hide the thing you are looking for.
contrast: A live aggregated view, usually over a rolling window
Spotting that something is wrong, fast
Aggregation hides single events, and the window may have rolled past
A scheduled summary, generated and retained
Trends, and proving a state at a point in time
Summarised: the detail behind it may be gone
Establishing whether the exploited flaw was known and when
Not evidence of what happened, only of what was possible
Volume, retention cost, and gaps if never collected
mentor.rule: Dashboards and reports tell you where to look. Raw logs tell you what happened. An investigation that ends at the dashboard has ended at a summary of itself.
mentor.tell: A question asking which source best supports a reconstruction or a timeline, offering a dashboard or a report alongside raw log types.
mentor.trap: A vulnerability scan from before the incident is genuinely valuable, but as context rather than evidence: it shows the flaw existed and was known, not that anyone used it.
